description: Slot templates for the Build tab: each split x level x days preset as placeholder slots. A slot has a label, slot_type, an eligibility rule (resolved to explicit lists in templates-reference.json by tools/templates.py eligible()), a set range, a ranked default exercise and the preset_exercise it came from. v2 (round 2): defaults are the best-ranked eligible pick (tools/templates.py ranked(): shared ranker, goal Size, the template level, commercial gym profile, +0.10 modeled bonus for primary lifts on compound slots) that keeps the template at 0 non-info warnings; filling every slot with preset_exercise still reproduces the linked splits.json preset exactly.

ranking.type_bonus_note: Compound slots only. A modeled preference for primary lifts (heavier, more loadable) as the default; not a measurement.
ranking.selection: tools/templates.py choose_defaults(): day then slot order; best-ranked pick that is not already on that day, not used elsewhere in the template when an unused valid pick exists, and keeps 0 non-info program-check warnings.
ranking.reference: slot-defaults-reference.json (top 5 per slot under Size / intermediate / commercial)

philosophy: Four ways to organise a routine compete for the teaching default. Per-muscle weekly volume has the best evidence: meta-analyses find a graded dose-response between weekly sets and muscle growth, with diminishing returns at higher volumes (Schoenfeld 2017; Pelland 2026), so weekly sets per muscle are the main lever and the app's targets are built on them. Frequency matters mostly as a way to spread that volume: when weekly sets are equated, training a muscle more often adds little (Schoenfeld 2019), although an earlier volume-equated analysis favoured twice a week over once (Schoenfeld 2016), and splitting sets keeps each session productive. Movement-pattern balance (a push, a pull, a squat, a hinge and so on) is a coaching convention rather than a tested outcome; it is a useful scaffold because a few patterns cover the major muscles and keep pushing and pulling roughly even. Priority or bias specialization (extra sets for one or two muscles, fewer for the rest) is a modeled choice for lifters who already have a baseline to build on. The teaching default is therefore pattern-based slots that hit the per-muscle weekly volume targets, spread over about two days per muscle, with specialization offered later. These are planning models, not measurements of what any one person will grow.
teaching_default: pattern-based slots that hit per-muscle weekly volume targets, spread over about 2 days per muscle

slot_schema.label: slot label (movement or muscle), " (main)" on primary compound slots
slot_schema.slot_type: primary | accessory | isolation (exercise type the slot takes)

eligibility.slot: patterns.json slot the pick must count for (patterns.candidates: level filters for advanced / rare equipment, never custom)
eligibility.movement_pattern: rules.json movement_patterns value the pick must have
eligibility.types: allowed exercise types: compound slots take primary or accessory, other slots the preset tile type
eligibility.variant: compound slots only: rules.json patterns group the pick must belong to (horizontal_press, incline_press, dip, ...)
eligibility.primary_muscle: isolation / core / other slots only: swap.primary_muscle of the pick

slot_schema.sets: {default, min, max}: min = max(2, default-1), max = min(5, default+1), never excluding the default
slot_schema.default_rank: 1-based position of the default in the ranked list
slot_schema.preset_exercise: the splits.json preset tile this slot came from; always eligible

volume_check: Default fill: 0 non-info program-check warnings for every template and no muscle red. The muscles below sit amber (within 2 sets under the level minimum or up to 25% over the max) with the ranked defaults (recomputed in round 2); tuning sets inside the session caps (hard sets, 90-minute warning, 5 sets per exercise) could not move them into range without a new warning, so they stay as documented exceptions.
